stem: The image's sharp contrast between the degraded 'old way of life' and the bright Soviet future best illustrates which technique of Soviet propaganda?
stimulus: [Image reconstructed from its caption] A Soviet newspaper image captioned 'Old Way of Life,' published in Izvestiia on International Women's Day, March 8, 1930. The image contrasts two worlds: on one side, the pre-revolutionary peasant woman — bent and weary, burdened with endless domestic labor in a dark hut under the watchful eyes of a stern husband and a priest; on the other, the new Soviet woman the state promised — upright and confident, a collective-farm worker and tractor driver striding toward a bright socialist future.
options: (A) Praising the achievements of the tsarist era.
(B) Presenting the revolution as a break from a backward past.
(C) Urging women to return to traditional domestic roles in the home.
(D) Criticizing the Five-Year Plan as a failure.
explanation: The image works by 'before and after': the old world is dark, priest-ridden drudgery; the new world is light and liberation — teaching viewers that everything good began with the revolution.

stem: The map presents the cable routes as one British system binding London to its Asian empire. Britain's investment in this network best illustrates which of the following about nineteenth-century imperialism?
stimulus: [Map reconstructed from its caption] A map of British undersea telegraph cables, circa 1870. Bold lines trace the cable routes from Britain across the Mediterranean to Alexandria in Egypt, then overland through Egypt to Suez, down the Red Sea to Aden, and across the Arabian Sea to Karachi and Bombay in India, with onward lines to Madras, Singapore, and Australia; a branch runs up the Persian Gulf. The map presents the whole network as a single British system binding London to its empire in Asia.
options: (A) The cables were built entirely by the independent governments of the colonies they served.
(B) Britain abandoned territorial empire in favor of purely commercial relationships.
(C) Imperial power depended on communications infrastructure as well as on soldiers and administrators.
(D) The telegraph immediately ended all resistance to British rule in Asia.
explanation: Submarine cables let London receive news from India in hours instead of months and issue orders the same day, shrinking the autonomy of distant officials. Building and defending this system was a deliberate imperial strategy: holding a global empire required not just garrisons and governors but the wires that kept them under central direction.

stem: Mao's repeated invocation of the 'worker-peasant alliance' most directly reflects which of the following?
stimulus: In recent years the spontaneous forces of capitalism have steadily grown in our countryside: new rich peasants spring up everywhere, and many well-to-do middle peasants strive to become rich peasants. Meanwhile many poor peasants still live in poverty for lack of sufficient means of production, some in debt and others selling or renting out their land. If this tendency goes unchecked, the polarization of the countryside will inevitably grow worse day by day. The peasants who lose their land and those who remain in poverty will complain that we do nothing to save them from ruin; nor will the well-to-do middle peasants heading down the capitalist road be pleased with us, for we can never satisfy their demands unless we take the capitalist road ourselves. Can the worker-peasant alliance continue to stand in these circumstances? Obviously not. There is no solution except on a new basis: to bring about, step by step, the socialist transformation of the whole of agriculture, together with socialist industrialization and the socialist transformation of handicrafts and capitalist industry and commerce — in other words, to carry out cooperation and eliminate the rich-peasant economy and the individual economy in the countryside, so that all rural people grow well-off together. This alone will consolidate the worker-peasant alliance. — Mao Zedong, On the Question of Agricultural Cooperation, 1955
options: (A) The Party's claim to represent both urban workers and rural peasants.
(B) A formal military alliance between China and the Soviet Union.
(C) A treaty between Chinese factory workers and peasant armies.
(D) The administrative merger of every factory with a neighboring farm collective.
explanation: The phrase is the party's legitimating formula: it rules in the name of workers and peasants together, so Mao frames collectivization as necessary to keep that coalition intact.

stem: China used paper currency centuries before any other civilization. Which of the following developments best explains why paper money emerged in China first?
stimulus: Image: a Ming dynasty paper banknote (baochao) issued under the Hongwu Emperor, c. 1375. The large rectangular note is printed with Chinese characters stating its denomination - one string (1,000 copper cash) - and bordered with a pattern of interlocking coins. An official red seal is stamped at the center. A printed warning reads: "Counterfeiters shall be decapitated; informers shall receive a reward of 250 taels of silver." Source: British Museum.
options: (A) China had no metal with which to make coins.
(B) European merchants demanded that China adopt paper money for their trade.
(C) China's commercial economy generated transaction volumes suited to paper.
(D) The Chinese government banned all forms of trade.
explanation: Paper money is awkward for small, simple economies but ideal for a large commercial one: it is light, easy to transport in bulk, and convenient for the high volume of transactions generated by China's markets, long-distance trade, and tax system.

explanation: A paper note is worthless in itself — its value rests entirely on public confidence that it will be accepted. Counterfeiting destroys that confidence, so the state treated it as an attack on the currency system itself, punishable by death.

stem: The map shows both the trans-Saharan trade of West Africa and the Indian Ocean trade of East Africa. Which of the following best describes a difference between these two trading systems?

The Sahara Desert lies to the north, crossed by caravan routes linking the Sahel to Mediterranean ports. In East and southern Africa: the Swahili city-states (1400s), including Mogadishu, Kilwa, and Sofala on the Indian Ocean coast, and Great Zimbabwe (1300s-1400s) in the interior. Also shown: the Red Sea, the Nile River, the Zambezi and Limpopo Rivers, and the Kalahari Desert. Trade routes connect gold-producing interior regions to both Saharan and Indian Ocean outlets.

explanation: The two systems used different transport suited to their geography: West African trade crossed the Sahara on camel caravans, while East African trade sailed the Indian Ocean on seasonal monsoon winds. Both moved gold and other goods, but one by land and the other by sea.

stem: Based on the passage, what did the Mongol relay system described by Marco Polo primarily demonstrate about the Mongol Empire?

explanation: A relay network spanning the whole empire, with fresh horses and standardized stations, is state infrastructure: it let one ruler send orders and receive news across thousands of miles, holding a vast and diverse realm together.

stem: Busbecq describes European forces as divided and demoralized while the Ottomans are disciplined and united. Which of the following sixteenth-century developments best explains the European disarray he observed?

stem: Guaman Poma, an indigenous Andean, writes in Spanish to the Spanish king while holding colonial offices. What does this best demonstrate about Spanish colonial society?

stem: Addams argues that women need the vote in order to carry out their "traditional responsibility" to children. What political strategy does this argument reflect?

(B) Demanding the immediate overthrow of the government.

(D) Presenting suffrage as an extension of women's domestic roles.
explanation: Rather than demanding rights as equals, Addams argues that women's traditional duties as mothers and moral guardians require the ballot. This maternalist framing made suffrage seem like a natural extension of womanhood rather than a radical break with it.

stem: Which of the following best explains why the League of Nations failed to stop Italy's invasion of Ethiopia?

explanation: The League's fatal weakness was structural: the United States never joined, and the League had no army or enforcement mechanism beyond economic sanctions that members applied half-heartedly. Italy correctly calculated that it could invade with impunity.

stem: The manifesto's explanation for the fall of the Yuan dynasty relies most heavily on which of the following ideas?

stem: The decision to send this manifesto to the Byzantine emperor best illustrates which of the following about the early Ming dynasty?

Since the Sung dynasty had lost the throne and Heaven had cut off their sacrifice, the Yuan dynasty had risen from the desert to enter and rule over China for more than a hundred years, when Heaven, wearied of their misgovernment and debauchery, thought also fit to turn their fate to ruin, and the affairs of China were in a state of disorder for eighteen years. But when the nation began to arouse itself, We conceived the patriotic idea to save the people, and it pleased the Creator to grant that Our civil and military officers effected their passage across the River. We have then been engaged in war for fourteen years; We have established peace in the Empire, and restored the old boundaries of China. We were selected by Our people to occupy the Imperial throne under the dynastic title of 'the Great Ming.' We now send a native of your country to hand you this Manifesto. Although We are not equal in wisdom to our ancient rulers, We cannot but let the world know Our intention to maintain peace within the four seas.

Source: Manifesto of Accession as First Ming Emperor, 1372 (sent to the Byzantine emperor)
options: (A) The new dynasty was announcing its legitimacy to foreign rulers within China's diplomatic order.
(B) The Ming sought a military alliance with Byzantium against the remaining Mongols.
(C) The manifesto was a declaration of war against the Byzantine Empire.
(D) The Ming emperor was proposing a new commercial treaty with Byzantium.
explanation: A new dynasty announcing itself to a distant foreign court was performing legitimacy: the Ming were declaring that the proper Chinese order had been restored and that foreign rulers should recognize the new Son of Heaven within the traditional diplomatic framework.

stem: Rubruck's comparison of Karakorum to the village and monastery of Saint Denis best illustrates which of the following?
stimulus:
'As for the city of Karacorum I can tell you that, not counting the Khan's palace, it is not as large as the village of Saint Denis, and the monastery of Saint Denis is worth ten times more than that palace. stem: Marco Polo's detailed account of the night-watch system in Kinsay most clearly demonstrates which of the following about Yuan-dynasty administration?
stimulus:
The people are Idolaters; and since they were conquered by the Great Kaan they use paper-money. Both men and women are fair and comely, and for the most part clothe themselves in silk, so vast is the supply of that material, both from the whole district of Kinsay, and from the imports by traders from other provinces. And you must know they eat every kind of flesh, even that of dogs and other unclean beasts, which nothing would induce a Christian to eat.

Since the Great Kaan occupied the city he has ordained that each of the 12,000 bridges should be provided with a guard of ten men, in case of any disturbance, or of any being so rash as to plot treason or insurrection against him. Each guard is provided with a hollow instrument of wood and with a metal basin, and with a time-keeper to enable them to know the hour of the day or night. And so when one hour of the night is past the sentry strikes one on the wooden instrument and on the basin, so that the whole quarter of the city is made aware that one hour of the night is gone. At the second hour he gives two strokes, and so on, keeping always wide awake and on the look out. In the morning again, from the sunrise, they begin to count anew, and strike one hour as they did in the night, and so on hour after hour.

Source: The Glories of Kinsay [Hangchow], Marco Polo, c. 1300
options: (A) The Mongol government left Chinese city administration entirely to local officials.
(B) The Yuan state relied mainly on religious authorities to keep the urban peace.
(C) Kinsay's government focused primarily on regulating foreign merchants.
(D) Urban policing in Kinsay was a routinized, centrally directed system for order.
explanation: Polo describes thousands of guards posted at every bridge, equipped with sounding instruments and timekeepers, striking the hours through the night by a fixed routine, which shows a highly organized administrative apparatus directed from the top.

stem: Polo's description of the people of Kinsay as 'Idolaters' who eat flesh 'which nothing would induce a Christian to eat' best illustrates which of the following?

The new Imperialism has nowhere extended the political and civil liberties of the mother country to any part of the vast territories which, since 1870, have fallen under the government of Western civilized Powers. Politically, the new Imperialism is an expansion of autocracy.

explanation: Hobson wrote a blistering critique of empire, yet he casually describes colonized peoples as 'lower races' incapable of self-government, showing that the racial hierarchies of 1902 shaped even the thinking of imperialism's opponents.
